content: The programs typically last four years and commence after the completion of secondary school Year 12. Upon successful completion, a Bachelor's degree is conferred by the affiliated university of the respective college. Engineering and medical colleges offer degree programs lasting four and five years, respectively, for Bachelor's degrees such as BE, BArch, BTech (following a three-year Diploma of Associate Engineer), and MBBS, which also begin after secondary school Year 12. The BTech (Honors) degree is considered equivalent and compatible with BE or BSc Engineering. The Bachelor of Architecture (BArch) program spans five years. In the Philippines, the term course is commonly used to refer to a Bachelor's degree. The most prevalent undergraduate degrees are the Bachelor of Science (BS) and Bachelor of Arts (AB or BA). Specializations, often referred to as majors, in fields such as economics, business administration, radiologic technology, nursing, architecture, and engineering are generally categorized under Science in most colleges and universities. Notably, architecture and engineering specializations require five years of study, unlike the standard four years for other programs. Other common degrees include the Bachelor in Education (BEd) and the Bachelor of Laws (LLB), the latter being a graduate degree. Following the American system, universities and colleges in the Philippines offer graduation with honors, such as cum laude, magna cum laude, and summa cum laude. In Europe, Bachelor's degrees are available in nearly every country. However, in some Continental European countries, these degrees were only recently introduced as part of the Bologna Process, where Bachelor's degrees were previously unknown. In Austria, the historical academic structure closely resembles that of Germany. Traditional first degrees included the Magister and the Diplom. In 2002, new educational legislation reintroduced the Bachelor's degree, which is awarded after three years of study. In Belgium, the Bologna Process replaced the old three-year grad school system with a three-year Bachelor's curriculum. This system also replaced the older twoor three-year candidatures, which prepared students for university diplomas. In Denmark, the Bachelor's degree was reintroduced in 1993 after the original baccalaureus degree was discontinued in 1775. The degree is awarded after three years of university study. Two types of Bachelor's degrees are currently offered: the Bachelor of Science (BSc), focusing on scientific, medical, or technical fields, and the Bachelor of Arts (BA), focusing on humanistic, theological, or jurisprudence areas. Since the late 1990s, Bachelor's degrees have also been introduced in fields like nursing and teaching. These are often referred to as profession-bachelor degrees and typically require four years of study at a college. However, these degrees do not automatically grant access to a Master's program, unlike traditional university-awarded Bachelor's degrees. In France, the traditional Bachelor's degree is equivalent to the French Licence, a three-year degree. Since the 2004 European LMD Bologna Process, universities offer a three-year Bachelor's degree, a two-year Master's degree, and a three-year or longer Doctorate program. In Germany, Bachelor's degrees, historically known as Bakkalaureus, were abolished in 1820 during educational reforms. The Magister degree, originally a graduate degree, became the first degree after five years of study. In 1899, the Diplom degree was introduced when technical universities gained university status. In 1998, new educational legislation reintroduced the Bachelor's degree as the first degree after three years of study. These degrees are now commonly referred to as either Bakkalaureus or Bachelor, with the English term being more widely used. Traditional degrees were phased out by 2010. In Italy, the Bologna Process replaced the old five-year laurea system. The current Bachelor's level corresponds to the Laurea, which typically takes three years to complete. Students must earn 180 credits and write a thesis to graduate. Graduation marks range from 66 to 110, with some universities awarding a maximum of 100. A distinction, or lode, may be granted to students achieving a perfect score of 110/110. Bachelor's and Master's graduates in Italy are addressed as Dottore (for men) or Dottoressa (for women). In the Netherlands, the degree system was restructured in 2004 to align with international standards. Former degrees such as baccalaureus (bc), doctorandus (drs), ingenieur (ing or ir), meester in de rechten (mr), and doctor (dr) are still awarded alongside their international equivalents. Bachelor's degrees are granted by both accredited colleges and universities. College Bachelor's degrees typically require four years of study, while university Bachelor's degrees require three years. University Bachelor's degrees allow direct entry into Master's programs, whereas college Bachelor's degrees often require an additional bridge year or pre-Master's year to qualify for Master's programs. In Poland, the licencjat degree is equivalent to the Bachelor's degree in Anglophone countries. In Russia and Ukraine, the specialist degree was the primary academic distinction in the Soviet Union. In the early 1990s, the Bakalavr (Bachelor's) degree was introduced across the Commonwealth of Independent States, except Turkmenistan. After earning a Bakalavr degree, students can pursue a Master's degree (requiring an additional 1–2 years) while retaining the old five-year specialist scheme. However, the specialist degree is being phased out in universities participating in the Bologna Process. In Switzerland, similar to Austria and Germany, there was no tradition of Bachelor's degrees. Traditional first degrees included the Licentiate and the Diplom, while second degrees included the DEA and the Postgraduate Diploma. Bachelor's and Master's degrees replaced the old degrees in 2003.
